newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian campaigners say decree to preserve Abacha.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian campaigners say decree to preserve Abacha.

text.p: Nigerian democracy campaigners on Thursday said a decree giving military ruler General Sani Abacha new powers showed he intended to stay in office through his plan to restore civilian rule.
Details of the new decree, which emerged in local newspapers, said Abacha was given absolute power over local governments elected in a March multiparty ballot.

"It shows the transition programme of General Abacha is designed by him and for him and lacks all semblance of a democratic process," human rights lawyer and democracy campaigner Gani Fawehinmi told Reuters.
Newspapers said the decree on local councils elected last month was issued by the ruling military council on Wednesday.

The semi-official Daily Times said under the decree the head of state could remove any local council head if he "is satisfied that the affairs of the council are not being managed in the best interest of the community or in any way to strengthen the unity of the people of Nigeria".
The decree says no civil court can challenge the validity of the election or the decision of a special election tribunal.

Nigeria's ruling generals hold up the peaceful conduct of the local elections as a sign of popular support for their plan to restore civilian rule by October 1998, despite criticism from pro-democracy campaigners.

The March ballot was the first multiparty election in Nigeria since a former military government annuled 1993 elections that would have ended 10 years of army rule and paved the way for Abacha to take over in ensuing political chaos.

At least two of five political parties permitted under the transition to democracy are actively seeking the infantry general as a candidate for the 1998 presidential elections, although he has not yet said he will stand.
"If there is a decree to allow Abacha to remove local governments elected by the people then will he not do the same if anybody were to challenge him?" asked Fawehinmi.
"These are signs that we are going on a journey without a destination."
If Abacha stood for election he would be following in the footsteps of other West African military leaders who have sought election as civilian rulers -- and in almost all cases won.
Diplomats from Western countries critical of Nigeria's human rights record and the slow pace of democractic reform were also cool to the new decree, but expressed litle surprise.

"When everything already seemed to have been sewn up and parties are virtually hand-picked anyway it hardly seems necessary to have a new decree just to make absolutely sure," said one western diplomat.

Despite heaping criticism on Nigeria's government, western countries have never seriously considered sanctions on lifeline crude oil exports or other measures that could hurt business interests in sub-Saharan Africa's largest economy.
